articles.title: The News That Arrived Two and a Half Years Late
articles.dek: In 1865, a quarter of a million people in Texas learned they had been free for years. The apostle John wrote to frightened believers for the same reason: life with God was already theirs, and they needed to hear it.
articles.quote: God's gift of life is already signed and settled; John wrote so that the news would reach the place where you actually live.
articles.body:
On June 18, 1865, a Union general named Gordon Granger landed at Galveston, a port town on the coast of Texas, with his troops. The next morning his headquarters issued a short document called General Order No. 3, and its opening sentence was read and posted for the town to hear: "The people of Texas are informed that, in accordance with a proclamation from the Executive of the United States, all slaves are free." Word moved outward from Galveston to the plantations and farms, and over the following weeks people began laying down their tools.

The freedom Granger announced was already two and a half years old. President Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation had taken effect on January 1, 1863, and it named Texas among the states where enslaved people were declared free. Texas, however, was remote, the Union army had not yet reached it, and many enslavers kept the news to themselves. For about thirty months, roughly a quarter of a million people kept rising before dawn and working the fields as though nothing had changed. Their freedom had been declared at the highest level, and it had simply never reached them.

What happened after the news arrived is one of the happiest chapters in American history. Freed men and women set out on the roads to search for husbands, wives, and children who had been sold away. In 1872 a group of them, led by a Baptist pastor named Jack Yates, pooled $800 and bought ten acres of land in Houston so they would always have a place to celebrate the day. They called it Emancipation Park. The day itself became known as Juneteenth, and it is now a national holiday in the United States. Any Filipino family that has waited for word from a loved one abroad understands what those people discovered: knowing the truth changes how you live, even when the truth has been settled for a long time.

Nearly two thousand years ago, an old man wrote a letter for the same reason. Early church tradition places the apostle John in Ephesus near the end of the first century, caring for a network of congregations in the region. Those churches had just been through a painful split. "They went out from us, but they did not really belong to us," John writes (1 John 2:19). The departing teachers seem to have claimed a higher spiritual knowledge, and they denied that Jesus had truly come in the flesh (1 John 4:2–3). Picture the house church the Sunday after they left. There are empty places on the benches. A teacher you once admired is now telling people across town that your faith is shallow and incomplete. A friend who used to greet you in the market looks the other way. The people who stayed are left with a quiet, frightening question: do we really have life with God, or were we fooled?

John answers like a lawyer calling witnesses. In the space of six verses (1 John 5:6–11), the Greek word for testimony, martyria, and its verb appear about ten times. It is courtroom language, the word from which we get "martyr," someone whose witness is so firm they will stake their life on it. John reminds his readers that they accept the word of ordinary witnesses every day, and then he raises the stakes: "We accept human testimony, but God's testimony is greater because it is the testimony of God, which he has given about his Son" (1 John 5:9). Then he tells them exactly what God has testified: "And this is the testimony: God has given us eternal life, and this life is in his Son" (1 John 5:11). The verdict is simple enough for a child to repeat: "Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life" (1 John 5:12). Then comes the sentence that explains why he wrote the whole letter.

"I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God so that you may know that you have eternal life." (1 John 5:13, NIV)

This verse becomes even richer when you set it beside the closing lines of John's Gospel. There he wrote, "These are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name" (John 20:31). The Gospel was written so that people would come to believe. This letter was written to people who already believed ("to you who believe"), so that they would know. The Greek word John uses, eidēte, comes from oida, a word for settled, confident knowledge, the way you know your own mother's voice. The verb "have" is in the present tense: you have eternal life now, today, while you are reading this.

One way to read this is that John saw his frightened friends living like the people of Texas before June 19. The life of God had been given to them. It was declared in heaven, sealed by the blood of Jesus, and confirmed by the Spirit (1 John 5:6–8). Yet many of them were still rising each morning with the anxious heart of someone who has to earn their place. John's letter is his General Order No. 3. He sends it so the news will finally reach the fields where they work. Our assurance rests on what God has said about his Son, and his word stands even on the mornings when our feelings are weak. That is why the letter ends with a burst of confidence, and John repeats the phrase "We know" in verses 18, 19, and 20.

God's gift of life is already signed and settled; John wrote so that the news would reach the place where you actually live. Many sincere Christians love Jesus and still carry a low, steady fear that God is disappointed in them, or that one more failure will close the door. They pray hesitantly, as though they were asking a stranger for a favor. John speaks straight to that heart. The very next thing he says is, "This is the confidence we have in approaching God: that if we ask anything according to his will, he hears us" (1 John 5:14). Assurance is the doorway to bold prayer. A person who knows they are a beloved child will speak to the Father freely and often.

This knowledge also explains the strange, abrupt last line of the letter: "Dear children, keep yourselves from idols" (1 John 5:21). An idol is anything we lean on to feel secure before God or before other people. When we are unsure of God's verdict, we reach for substitutes, such as a spotless record, the approval of others, a busy ministry, or a bank balance that finally feels safe. Each of these promises the peace that God has already given in his Son. John's tender closing reminds us that people who know they are free have no need to keep serving the old masters.

The freedmen of Houston understood that good news needs a place to be remembered, so they bought land and returned to it every year. You can do something similar in a smaller way. Write 1 John 5:11–13 on a card, put it where you will see it each morning, and read it aloud when doubt or guilt comes calling, the way the order was read aloud in Galveston. Let the words remind you that the verdict was given before you ever heard it, by a Witness who cannot lie. Then go into your day as a free person. If you have the Son, you have life, and God has written to make sure you know it.

articles.title: The Teachers Who Shine Like Stars
articles.dek: Daniel's darkest vision is crowded with kings and armies. When God finally names the people who will shine forever, he names the ones who helped others understand.
articles.quote: In God's eyes, the brightest life is the one that helps someone else see.
articles.body:
In 1930, an American missionary named Frank Laubach was living beside Lake Lanao in Mindanao, in the town then called Dansalan, which we now know as Marawi. He had served in the Philippines since 1915, and by his own account he was lonely and discouraged. So he began a private experiment, trying to turn his thoughts toward God every waking minute, and the letters he wrote about it later became a small spiritual classic. Out of that season of prayer came a very practical burden for his Maranao neighbors, most of whom could not read.

Working alongside Maranao helpers, Laubach built simple charts that linked familiar words and pictures to the sounds of their own language. A grown man could learn the syllables in an afternoon and begin reading within days. There were never enough paid teachers, so each new reader was asked to pass the gift along to someone else, and the phrase "Each one teach one" was born. The method traveled from the shores of Lake Lanao to India, Africa and Latin America, and it is commonly credited with helping tens of millions of people learn to read. It all began with one discouraged man deciding that the most useful thing he could do in a forgotten corner of the world was to help the person in front of him understand.

That same instinct turns out to be the hero of one of the strangest chapters in the Bible. Daniel 11 and 12 form the close of a single long vision that came to Daniel "in the third year of Cyrus king of Persia" (Daniel 10:1). By then Daniel was an old man who had spent nearly his whole life as an exile in Babylon. A heavenly messenger came to show him what lay ahead for his people, and what he saw was a parade of kings.

The vision moves at dizzying speed. Persian kings rise, and then "a mighty king" appears whose empire is "broken up and parceled out toward the four winds of heaven" (Daniel 11:3–4), which most readers have long connected with Alexander the Great and the splitting of his empire after his death. After that, a "king of the North" and a "king of the South" march back and forth for generations, arranging marriages, breaking treaties and wearing down each other's armies. Historians recognize in these lines the long rivalry between the Seleucid kings of Syria and the Ptolemies of Egypt, with the small land of Judea caught between them like a modest house wedged between two quarrelling neighbors.

Then the vision slows down for "a contemptible person" who seizes power through intrigue (Daniel 11:21). Most interpreters, Jewish and Christian alike, identify him with Antiochus IV, who in 167 BC outlawed Jewish worship and set up a pagan altar in the temple in Jerusalem, the event Daniel calls "the abomination that causes desolation" (Daniel 11:31). For faithful Jews this was the darkest night imaginable, a time when keeping God's law could cost you your life.

At that very point the vision turns its attention away from the palace and toward a different kind of person entirely. "The people who know their God will firmly resist him," the messenger says. "Those who are wise will instruct many, though for a time they will fall by the sword or be burned or captured or plundered" (Daniel 11:32–33). After more turmoil, after a promise that the archangel Michael will stand guard over God's people and that "multitudes who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake" (Daniel 12:1–2), the whole vision reaches its high point with these words:

"Those who are wise will shine like the brightness of the heavens, and those who lead many to righteousness, like the stars for ever and ever." (Daniel 12:3)

The Hebrew word behind "those who are wise" is maskilim, from a root that means to have insight or to act with understanding. It appears near the very beginning of the book, when young Daniel and his friends are chosen for the Babylonian court because they show "aptitude for every kind of learning" (Daniel 1:4). The same word that described a group of captive teenagers now describes the heroes of the last days. In chapter 11, the phrase translated "will instruct many" means, quite literally, "will make many understand." The maskilim are people whose wisdom flows outward. They explain, they encourage and they help frightened neighbors see what God is doing when nothing seems to make sense.

This turns the whole chapter around. For forty-some verses, greatness has been measured in territory, armies and alliances. Antiochus even gave himself the title Epiphanes, meaning "God made manifest," though the ancient historian Polybius reports that some people mocked him behind his back as Epimanes, "the madman." Today his name survives mostly in footnotes. The teachers who helped their neighbors hold on to God in those years are almost all unnamed, yet they are the ones God promises will shine "for ever and ever." In God's eyes, the brightest life is the one that helps someone else see.

There is a second echo worth hearing. The phrase "lead many to righteousness" closely resembles Isaiah's description of the suffering Servant, of whom God says, "my righteous servant will justify many" (Isaiah 53:11). Many scholars think Daniel is deliberately borrowing that language, so the humble teachers of Daniel 12 share in the Servant's work in a small way. Christians see that work fulfilled in Jesus, and the New Testament picks up the same image when Paul tells ordinary believers in Philippi that they will "shine among them like stars in the sky" (Philippians 2:15). A star is valued for the light it gives to travelers in the dark, which is exactly how Daniel pictures the wise.

The passage is also honest about the cost and about human weakness. "Some of the wise will stumble," the messenger admits, "so that they may be refined, purified and made spotless until the time of the end" (Daniel 11:35). The people who help others understand are themselves still learning, and they sometimes fall. God does not disqualify them for it. He uses even their stumbling to make them purer, and their light keeps reaching others.

Most of us will never command armies or appear in history books, and Daniel 12 suggests that this is no loss at all. Think of the people who made you understand something of God: a lola who taught you to pray before meals, a Sunday school teacher who stayed after class, a friend who sat with you in the hospital and opened the Psalms. They probably never thought of themselves as wise, but heaven did. Their kind of wisdom is relational, passed from one life to another the way Laubach's charts were passed from one reader to the next.

You can take your place in that line this week by choosing one person and helping them understand one good thing. It might mean reading a short psalm with your child at bedtime, explaining a verse to a coworker who is curious, or patiently showing an aging parent how to join the online prayer meeting. It might simply mean telling someone who is afraid, in plain words, why you still trust God. None of these acts looks impressive, and each of them is the very thing Daniel saw shining in the heavens.

The vision ends with a gentle word to an old man who had been faithful for a very long time. "As for you, go your way till the end," the messenger tells him. "You will rest, and then at the end of the days you will rise to receive your allotted inheritance" (Daniel 12:13). Daniel did not have to understand every detail of the kings and their wars, and neither do you. Go your way today, help one person see a little more clearly, and trust that the God who counts the stars has not overlooked a single light you have kindled.

articles.title: The Forest They Had Never Seen
articles.dek: Every autumn, millions of monarch butterflies fly to a mountain forest that none of them has ever visited. Psalm 135 was sung by people who found their way home in the same manner.
articles.quote: Faith travels the way the monarchs do, carried by those who never saw the beginning toward a home they have been promised.
articles.illustration: monarch butterflies' multigenerational migration to Mexico
articles.body:
Every autumn, high in the mountains west of Mexico City, the oyamel fir forests begin to change color, though the change has nothing to do with their needles. By late November, millions of monarch butterflies have settled on the branches in clusters so thick that the limbs bend under their weight, and whenever the sun warms them the whole forest seems to breathe orange. Some of them have flown close to four thousand kilometers from Canada and the northern United States to reach those slopes. For most of the twentieth century, scientists did not know where the eastern monarchs went in winter, until 1975, when Ken Brugger and Catalina Aguado, searching on behalf of the Canadian zoologist Fred Urquhart, found the colonies resting quietly in the cold mountain air.

The most surprising part of the story came afterward. None of the butterflies in those trees has ever been there before. A summer monarch lives only a few weeks, so the butterflies that leave Mexico in spring lay eggs on their way north, and their children lay eggs, and so on across three or four generations spread over a continent. The ones that fly south each autumn belong to a special long-lived generation that can survive up to eight months, and they are the great-grandchildren, sometimes the great-great-grandchildren, of the last butterflies to see that mountain. Researchers have learned that they steer by the sun, adjusting for its movement across the sky with a tiny clock kept partly in their antennae. With no parent to follow and no memory of the place, they still arrive in the very forests their ancestors left.

I thought of those butterflies while reading Psalm 135, because it is a song sung by people who were never there either. Its opening lines call to "you who minister in the house of the LORD, in the courts of the house of our God" (Psalm 135:2). It was written for temple worship, and many scholars believe it took its final shape after the exile, when a small and weary community had come back from Babylon to a modest rebuilt temple under foreign rule. Moses had been dead for centuries. Nobody in that choir had seen the sea divide or tasted manna in the desert. And yet, standing in the courtyard, they began to sing about Egypt as if it had happened that morning.

The psalmist moves quickly, the way a family flips through an old album. "He struck down the firstborn of Egypt, the firstborn of people and animals" (Psalm 135:8). It is a sobering line, and the psalm does not gloat over it; it simply names the night of grief when a stubborn empire finally let enslaved families walk free. Then the singer turns and speaks to Egypt directly, in the present tense of a witness: "He sent his signs and wonders into your midst, Egypt, against Pharaoh and all his servants" (Psalm 135:9). The story moves on to the wilderness road and the kings who tried to block it, "Sihon king of the Amorites, Og king of Bashan, and all the kings of Canaan" (Psalm 135:11). Israel remembered Og especially as a giant of a man, and Deuteronomy notes, almost with a smile, that his iron bed was "nine cubits long" (Deuteronomy 3:11), about four meters. Finally God "gave their land as an inheritance, an inheritance to his people Israel" (Psalm 135:12). The Hebrew word there, nachalah, is the word for a family's portion, the field a father leaves to his children and they leave to theirs.

Then the choir lifts its eyes from the album and sings the lines that the whole history was leading toward.

"Your name, LORD, endures forever, your renown, LORD, through all generations. For the LORD will vindicate his people and have compassion on his servants." (Psalm 135:13–14)

Verse 13 is an echo, and the original hearers would have caught it at once. At the burning bush, when Moses asked God for his name, God answered, "This is my name forever, the name you shall call me from generation to generation" (Exodus 3:15). The Hebrew in both places pairs two words: shem, meaning name, and zeker, which the NIV renders "renown" but which more literally means remembrance, the name people call out when they remember what someone has done. At the bush, God handed Moses a name meant to be passed down. Psalm 135 is the evidence that it was. Centuries later, a choir that had never seen a plague or crossed a sea still knew the name and still knew the way, carried along by remembrance much as the monarchs are carried by a direction they never personally learned.

Verse 14 is borrowed too. It comes almost word for word from the song Moses taught Israel just before he died (Deuteronomy 32:36). The verb translated "vindicate," din, means to judge or to take up someone's case, the way an advocate stands beside a person who cannot defend themselves. The phrase "have compassion" comes from nacham, a word for comfort and for a deep change of heart toward someone. It is the same root God uses in Isaiah 40:1, "Comfort, comfort my people, says your God," a message spoken to exiles. One way to read the psalm, then, is that the singers remembered the past so they could trust God in their own present. The God who argued Israel's case before Pharaoh would argue theirs before Persia, and the compassion that met slaves in Egypt would meet tired returnees in a half-finished Jerusalem. The history lesson ends with a promise in the future tense.

The contrast arrives a few verses later, when the psalm turns to the idols of the nations, which "have mouths, but cannot speak, eyes, but cannot see" (Psalm 135:16). An idol has no story to tell and no one to remember. The LORD has a name that has been spoken over kitchen tables and temple courts for thousands of years, and every generation that speaks it adds another chapter of his faithfulness.

Many of us quietly worry that our faith is secondhand. We grew up on a lola's rosary at dawn, on a father's story of how God provided in the year the business failed, on a mother's prayer whispered over a fever. We may wonder whether we have had a Red Sea of our own, or whether we are only repeating someone else's experience. Psalm 135 suggests that inherited memory is exactly how God designed his name to travel. The choir in that courtyard did not apologize for singing about events they had never seen. They sang them boldly, because the God of those events was still listening, still taking up their case, still moved with compassion for his servants. The stories your elders gave you are your nachalah, a portion handed down with your name on it.

And you are also the generation that carries it forward. The psalm names Sihon and Og specifically, with places and details, because specific memories travel better than general ones. In these weeks before Simbang Gabi, when families gather early in the dark and the season turns toward Christmas, you might take a few minutes today to tell one younger person one particular time God was kind to your family, with names, dates, and the small details that made it real. A child who hears how God carried a grandparent through a hard season will someday know which way to fly when their own season grows cold.

Right now, the monarchs are resting in those mountain forests, wings folded, waiting out the winter together. In spring they will rise and head north, and their great-grandchildren will find their way back without ever having seen the place. Faith travels the way the monarchs do, carried by those who never saw the beginning toward a home they have been promised. If you feel small and tired this morning, take heart from that choir in the courtyard. The name they sang still endures, and the God it belongs to is still taking up the cause of his people and meeting his servants with compassion, including you.

articles.title: The Hunger That Makes Hard Words Sweet
articles.dek: Pixar learned that honest feedback only helps people who are hungry for it. Solomon said the same thing three thousand years earlier, and Jesus still offers that kind of honest counsel today.
articles.quote: The same honest word that one person tramples, another receives like honey, and the difference is rarely the word. It is the hunger.
articles.body:
In the early 1990s, a small studio in Northern California set out to do something no one had done: make a full-length movie entirely on computers. The people at Pixar were gifted, but they soon found a problem that talent alone could not solve. Every story they started was weak at the beginning. Years later, cofounder Ed Catmull put it bluntly in his book Creativity, Inc.: "Early on, all of our movies suck." He meant it as a plain description of how good work actually gets made.

So they built something unusual. A small circle of directors and storytellers, the people who had made Toy Story, began meeting regularly to watch one another's unfinished films and say honestly what was not working. They called it the Braintrust. It had no authority at all. It could not order a single change, and the director was free to ignore every note. Its only power was honesty from people who wanted the film to succeed. Catmull insisted that the notes be about the movie and never an attack on the filmmaker. Out of those uncomfortable rooms came films that Filipino families have watched again and again on Sunday afternoons, such as Finding Nemo, Up and Inside Out.

One part of the story is easy to miss. A system like that only helps a person who wants to hear what it says. A director who believes the film is already finished will hear every note as an insult. A director who knows the film is not there yet can hear the same note as rescue. The words in the room are identical, and what changes is the appetite of the person listening. An old proverb said exactly this about three thousand years before Pixar existed.

The book of Proverbs is mostly a father's wisdom collected for the young, and chapters 25 to 29 have a history of their own. They are "proverbs of Solomon, compiled by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah" (Proverbs 25:1). That means royal scribes, more than two centuries after Solomon, gathered these sayings because they thought their own generation needed them. Chapter 27 keeps coming back to friendship. Just before our passage, the sage writes, "Better is open rebuke than hidden love. Wounds from a friend can be trusted, but an enemy multiplies kisses" (Proverbs 27:5–6). Then he turns, rather surprisingly, to food.

"One who is full loathes honey from the comb, but to the hungry even what is bitter tastes sweet." (Proverbs 27:7)

On the surface this is a simple observation from the dinner table. After a big Christmas Eve Noche Buena, even the best leche flan gets pushed away. And anyone who has been truly hungry, after a long fast, a missed meal on a hard shift, or a season when money ran out, knows that plain rice with a little salt can taste like a feast. The Hebrew is even stronger than our English. Where the NIV says the full person "loathes" honey, the verb is bus, which means to trample or tread underfoot. A satisfied soul will walk right over the sweetest thing on the table.

The deeper connection shows up two verses later, and it is easy to miss in translation. Verse 9 reads, "Perfume and incense bring joy to the heart, and the pleasantness of a friend springs from their heartfelt advice" (Proverbs 27:9). The word translated "pleasantness" is meteq, which literally means sweetness. It comes from the same root as matoq, the "sweet" of verse 7. And the phrase "heartfelt advice" is literally "counsel of the soul," using nephesh, the same word for the hungry or full "one" in verse 7. Read together, the sayings suggest a picture. A true friend's honest counsel is the honey. Whether it tastes sweet depends on the soul receiving it. The full soul tramples it, while the hungry soul finds that even the bitter parts, the wound from verse 6, taste sweet.

This suggests that the real question is rarely whether we have wise people around us. Most of us do. We have a tita who sees what we cannot, a coworker who knows where our project is weak, a spouse who has noticed a pattern we keep repeating. The question is our appetite. Filipino culture has real strengths here, with our warmth and our pakikisama, the instinct to keep everyone at ease. Yet that same instinct can teach us to fill up on pleasant talk until we have no room left for a hard word. A friend senses the fullness and stops offering the honey.

The gospel goes right to this point. In Revelation, the risen Jesus speaks to a church in Laodicea, a wealthy city known for banking and textiles. The church says, "I am rich; I have acquired wealth and do not need a thing," and Jesus answers, "But you do not realize that you are wretched, pitiful, poor, blind and naked" (Revelation 3:17). That is about as bitter as a word can taste. Yet his next sentence is pure friendship: "I counsel you to buy from me gold refined in the fire, so you can become rich" (Revelation 3:18). Two verses later he says, "Here I am! I stand at the door and knock" (Revelation 3:20). The church was full, so it was trampling the honey, and Jesus loved them enough to tell them so.

Here is the good news hidden inside a proverb about appetite: hunger is a gift. Mary sang that God "has filled the hungry with good things but has sent the rich away empty" (Luke 1:53), and Jesus promised, "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be filled" (Matthew 5:6). Admitting that we are not finished, that our lives have scenes that still do not work, is where grace begins. The cross is the most bitter word ever spoken about human sin, and to a hungry heart it is also the sweetest news in the world. Jesus calls his followers "friends" (John 15:15), and like every true friend in Proverbs 27, he tells us the truth because he wants our story to end well.

The same honest word that one person tramples, another receives like honey, and the difference is rarely the word. It is the hunger. You do not have to wait for hard counsel to find you. Pixar's directors walked into the Braintrust on purpose, and you can do something similar this week by choosing one trusted friend who loves God and loves you, and asking a simple question over coffee or a message: "What is one thing you see in me that I might not see?" When the answer comes, resist the urge to explain or defend yourself. Say thank you, take it home, and bring it to the Lord in prayer.

Verse 10 adds a gentle footnote: "better a neighbor nearby than a relative far away" (Proverbs 27:10). The friends whose counsel helps most are usually the ones close enough to see your daily life, so look for them nearby. And if you find yourself pushing every hard word away today, treat that fullness as a signal, and ask God to make you hungry again. He has never once refused to feed a hungry soul, and the counsel he sends through his Word and his people may turn out to be the sweetest thing you taste all week.
